description: Grounds for Thought: Defence Colony, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Thursday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.3rd September: Dr. Rahul KapoorWomen, Work and Well BeingWomen's participation in paid and unpaid work shapes far more than a household budget, it shapes physical, psychological, economic, and social well-being all at once. But that participation is rarely on equal terms: wage gaps, occupational segregation, invisible care work, and the daily balancing act between job and family all take a toll. Dr. Rahul Kapoor, Assistant Professor of Sociology and Social Work at Gautam Buddha University and author of Women and Work: The Sky is Full of Sexism, asks what a genuinely gender-sensitive approach to employment and social protection would actually look like — and why economic participation alone was never going to be enough.17th September: Anukriti AgarwalChacha Knows Best: Chacha Chaudhary and the Politics of NostalgiaBefore Indian households had cable or the internet, they had Chacha Chaudhary — a turbaned uncle whose brain worked faster than a computer, created by Pran Kumar Sharma in 1971. Fifty years on, that same deliberately ordinary uncle now sells toilets, water conservation, and voter turnout on behalf of government ministries. Anukriti Agarwal, a language educator and Fulbright Fellow at Yale, traces how a comic-book uncle went from newsprint to nation-building — and what it reveals when a state borrows the nostalgia the middle class grew up on.24th September: Dr Shashank SinghPrinces in the Polls: Indian Royals and Inherited Power in a Democratic Age, 1948–1967Between the 1950s and 60s, former princely elites didn't disappear from Indian politics — they reinvented themselves within it. Dr Shashank Singh, Junior Fellow at the Prime Ministers Museum and Library and a historian of Gwalior's princely order, uses electoral data and legislative debate from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh to show how monarchical charisma and patronage fused with electoral legitimacy. His argument: India's democratic consolidation didn't dismantle the feudal order so much as absorb and repurpose it.

description: Grounds for Thought: Janpath, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Tuesday evenings. Prateek Mundeja, Assistant Professor of Political Science and Mookerjee Fellow (2025–26), argues that the more useful question is a duller one: what actually works? This session takes a realist's tour through limited resources, institutional capacity, and the gap between stated intentions and delivered outcomes — and makes the case that ideals only survive contact with the world when backed by hard, unglamorous choices.22nd September: Aarushee ShuklaThe Pause, The Buzzword, and The CollectiveIn a meeting room in Bihar and Kerala, Aarushee Shukla asked women what their collective meant to them, and got a long, deliberate silence back. That silence, she found, wasn't an absence of an answer — it was its own kind of answer, one we're rarely taught to read. This session recreates that pause live, then turns to the vocabulary — "empowerment," "participation," "social capital" — that runs through women's lives on paper, asking who gets to write those words and who is simply left to live inside them.29th September: Amitrajeet MukherjeeVoices from War: Revisiting John Keegan's The Face of BattleJohn Keegan's landmark book opened with a deceptively simple question — what is it actually like to be in a battle? Fifty years on, his witnesses remain almost entirely European, despite spanning centuries of warfare. Amitrajeet Mukherjee, a doctoral candidate in English Literature at Delhi University, widens that frame to the two and a half million Indians who served in the Second World War — diarists, letter-writers, the censored and the unrecorded — and asks whose voices get to define what "war writing" is for.

Hidden Heritage of Wazirpur invites participants to step beyond familiar heritage circuits and discover a landscape where silence has become both its greatest mystery and its greatest storyteller.The experience explores monuments that once stood at the heart of thriving settlements but gradually slipped from public memory as the city expanded around them. Through architectural observation, historical context, and field-based interpretation, participants uncover how these overlooked structures reveal stories of patronage, engineering, settlement patterns, and Delhi's evolving urban fabric. Equally, the walk raises important questions about conservation, memory, and the value we assign to heritage beyond UNESCO sites and celebrated monuments. It is an invitation to see the extraordinary in the overlooked and to recognise that every forgotten structure holds the potential to reshape our understanding of Delhi's past.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Delhi's forgotten heritage landscapes and the historical evolution of Wazirpur.Explore the Wazirpur Tomb Complex and understand its architectural significance.Visit hidden medieval tombs scattered across the landscape, discussing their patrons and forgotten histories.Examine surviving historic water systems and their importance in sustaining medieval settlements.Explore lesser-known medieval structures while interpreting architectural features and construction techniques.Discuss urbanisation, neglect and the conservation challenges facing Delhi's undocumented heritage.Encourage participants to observe, document and appreciate overlooked monuments as valuable cultural assets.Closing discussion and photography.

name: 'Doing' Literature: Intimacy, Risk, Pleasure
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that pushes back on everything school taught you about reading. Growing up, we're told that good exam results prove we've gained good knowledge of everything we've read. But we know that the markers of un-success, what we struggle with, what we can't fully express or understand, what we continue to puzzle over, remain the most memorable and meaningful of our engagements with reading.The humanities isn't about drawing a line under a problem with a QED. It isn't a formula that solves the troubles of the world, personal or political. It's about risk, intimacy, pleasure and failure, because it's an encounter with life itself.This lecture thinks through reading and translating literature, particularly poetry: the desire for it, the labour of it, the frustration and thrill of it, the failure and even death of it. Gayatri Spivak called translation "the most intimate act of reading"  a translator's complete surrender to the text. This talk goes further: reading itself is an intimate act, a constant jousting with everything that unsettles us, and translation only deepens it, an erotics that can go very right, or very wrong.The session explores:Why "un-success" is often reading's most meaningful outcomeWhat Gayatri Spivak meant by calling translation "the most intimate act of reading"How risk, intimacy, pleasure and failure define an authentic engagement with literatureWhy the humanities resist the comfort of formulas and easy resolutionsAbout the SpeakerBrinda Bose is Professor at the Centre for English Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University. She taught earlier at Delhi University and was a Fellow of the Nehru Memorial Museum and Library in New Delhi. She has been a Rockefeller Fellow at Bellagio, Italy, at the Humanities Center of Boston University, and at the Camargo Foundation in Cassis, France. Her interests span modernist and avant-garde literature, cinema and other arts, gender and sexualities, and translation. She completed her BA at Presidency College, Calcutta, a second BA and MA at the University of Oxford, and her PhD at Boston University, all in English literature. description: About the LectureThe Epics have held the Indian imagination since time immemorial, narrated, performed and rendered into cinema again and again. It strips away the proverbial sheen of the "just" war to focus on the human question underneath. Whether it's the fiery Draupadi, the "manipulative" Satyavati, the warrior queen Chitrangada, Janaki, or the duo of Kaikeyi and Manthara, the Epics allow us to deconstruct these women through a modern feminist lens.The session explores:How feminist retellings of the Mahabharata and Ramayana recentre their women charactersWhat writers like Tagore, Mahasweta Devi, Irawati Karve and Chitra Divakaruni reveal through their retellingsWhy the Epics' "timeless" characters remain contemporary and urgently relevantHow deconstructing canonical narratives changes what the stories are actually aboutAbout the SpeakerDr. Nandini C.
